then.text: Oh, it's you from the band. Did she send you? I split a top note on Whit Friday last year, right in front of the judge, and I've been hiding at Dovestone ever since.
You can't see the judge, you know. They sit in a car or a back room so they can't tell which band's which. Somehow that makes it worse.
...You're right. And it's only a march. Cornet up. I'll see you at the Band Room.

else.text: {greeting} Lovely and quiet at Dovestone. Just me, the reservoir and the occasional man with a very big camera lens.
Can't play down here though. The sheep get opinions.

then.text: Is this Saddleworth or Kinder? I've been walking the Pennine Way in this fog since Tuesday. The tuba is heavier than it looks, and it looks very heavy.
A mountain hare! Now I know where I am. The only wild ones in England live round here. Right, downhill it is. Tell them I'm coming.

else.text: Show me a mountain hare and I'll believe you. They only live wild on these moors in all of England. Find one in the heather and bring it here.
{greeting} Don't mind me. Just carrying a tuba along the Pennine Way. For training. It's a long story with a lot of hills in it.

moor_ranger.text: {greeting} Hear that bubbling call? Curlew. Back on the moor every spring. Biggest wading bird in Europe, that one, with a beak like a sickle.
Twenty years ago the peat up here was bare and black and washing away. We've been blocking the gullies and planting sphagnum moss by the hand-ful. It holds water like a sponge.
Wet peat stores carbon and slows the floods down in the valleys. Dry peat just blows away. So, please, keep to the flags.

moor_weaver.text: {greeting} I started at the mill at fourteen. You learnt to lip-read, because you'd never hear a word over the looms. Some of us still do it in the pub.
We wore clogs. Wooden soles, iron caulkers underneath. Sparked on the cobbles on a dark morning. Lovely sound, a street full of clogs at six o'clock.

moor_yorkie.text: {greeting} Manchester, the sign says. Yorkshire, I say. My postcode can say what it likes.
The Saddleworth Rushbearing's in August. We pull a cart piled with rushes round the villages, with a man sat on top. Sounds daft. It is daft. It's grand.

moor_poet.text: {greeting} First proper walk on the Pennine Way? Mind the bogs. If the ground wobbles, it's not the ground's fault.
Golden plover up by the edge this morning. Little sad whistle. They sound like they've lost their keys.

moor_leggers.text: {greeting} Leggers used to take boats through Standedge lying on their backs on boards, walking the roof of the tunnel. Three miles of that. Hours of it.
The horses went over the top on the Boat Lane, with a lad, and met the boat at the other end. Better view. Fewer bats.

moor_hare_spot.text: A mountain hare sits up in the heather, ears like two exclamation marks. It looks at you. It decides you are not a fox, and goes back to eating.

moor_wang_steward.text: Boots are in the barrel. Wind is from the west, which on Saddleworth means it is from everywhere.
